implementation_notes: TypeScript adds no ring buffer but its types make the fixed-size backing store explicit and the full/empty state a discriminated result rather than a magic sentinel - which is the main correctness improvement over a JavaScript ring. A fixed Float32Array/Uint8Array with wrapping head/tail indices is the same-thread ring (no atomics needed - the event loop is single-threaded); across workers, SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics gives the indices, and Atomics.wait (worker-only) makes it a blocking ring. For MPMC or blocking, the honest answer is not a hand-written ring but a library (e.g. a bounded AsyncQueue), because the CAS loop and lost-wakeup handling is where a hand-rolled ring goes wrong. The typed-array ring is the right choice for a numeric frame buffer with a fixed, known memory footprint.
idiom_name: fixed TypedArray ring with wrapping head/tail indices (same-thread) or SharedArrayBuffer+Atomics (across workers); typed discriminated results for full/empty
pitfalls: A normal Array with push/shift is the unbounded, allocating default; the Float32Array ring is the bounded, fixed-memory replacement.
Full and empty both give head === next unless one slot is wasted or a count is kept; the 'ok' | 'full' result type makes the policy explicit in the signature.
The capacity must be a power of two for the & mask wrap; a non-power-of-two size wraps wrongly with the mask.
Across workers, Atomics.wait throws on the browser main thread - the main thread polls, or the ring lives in a worker.
A hand-written MPMC ring in TypeScript needs a CAS loop (compareExchange) and is easy to get wrong; use a bounded library queue for multi-producer.
alternative: A bounded library queue (e.g. a bounded AsyncQueue) for multi-producer/consumer or blocking; the typed array ring is for a same-thread numeric frame buffer
